Social Studies.title: Social studies week 4: the Western Hemisphere today and civic issues
Social Studies.subject: Social Studies
Social Studies.contentMarkdown:
![Blank organizer for comparing civic evidence from two sources](images/grade-05/social-studies/g05-social-civic-issue-evidence-organizer.png)

**Review and self-check:** Explain the difference between a problem statement, evidence, and a proposed action in three separate sentences. **Check:** the problem identifies what is happening and where; evidence is traceable to a source; the action names who could do what. Have a partner highlight any sentence that mixes a personal opinion with a source fact. Rewrite it so the opinion is labeled and the fact has a citation. Keep copies of the actual assigned sources with the petition or presentation so the audience can verify the request.

**Verified course content:** The fourth Passport unit is “The Western Hemisphere Today.” Its public description says students study multiple perspectives on issues such as individual and social rights and the role of government, using primary and secondary sources, artifacts, paintings, photographs, and maps. The unit's full materials are restricted to NYCDOE login. Use the teacher's actual issue and assigned countries; this file does not choose an issue or invent local facts for students. [NYCDOE Grade 5 Unit 4](https://www.weteachnyc.org/resources/resource/passport-social-studies-grade-5-unit-3-f9d95712-e567-48f6-9582-36550c4c3164-copy/).

#### Public-source case study: monarch butterflies cross borders

**This is a real, sourced practice case, not a claim about the classroom assignment.** New York's Grade 5 framework asks students to investigate a current issue that two or more Western Hemisphere countries face together; it gives environmental issues as one example. The public Passport Unit 4 description also asks students to compare a present-day issue in two countries. This monarch case fits that published scope, but Nahid's actual class issue and country pair must still come from the teacher. [NYSED, Grade 5 Social Studies Framework, §5.5b](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/standards-instruction/ss-framework-k-8a2.pdf); [NYCDOE Unit 4 description](https://www.weteachnyc.org/resources/resource/passport-social-studies-grade-5-unit-3-f9d95712-e567-48f6-9582-36550c4c3164-copy/).

**Source reading — one butterfly, a long route, and shared work**

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) describes two North American migrating monarch groups. The eastern group spends winter in central Mexico. In spring, monarchs move north through the United States toward Canada over more than one generation. The western group has different winter sites, along the California coast. The groups should not be treated as if they all follow one identical path.

USFWS measures the eastern group's winter sites by the area the butterflies cover, in hectares. It measures the western group by the number of butterflies counted; a separate line on the western graph shows how many sites were surveyed. The report says the two groups can rise or fall from year to year, but the long records show declines at their winter sites. It identifies habitat loss and damage, insecticide exposure, and climate change among the main pressures. Read the full report's Figure 2.2 for the migration map and Figure E1 for the two different population measures. [USFWS, *Monarch Butterfly Species Status Assessment*, version 2.3 (December 2024)](https://www.fws.gov/sites/default/files/documents/2025-01/ssa_monarch-butterfly_2024.pdf).

UNESCO's World Heritage Committee records a different kind of evidence: a policy decision about the Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve in Mexico. Its 2025 decision recognizes cooperation among Canada, Mexico, and the United States and encourages the countries to protect habitat, reduce milkweed loss, and work together along the migration corridor. That wording is a recommendation. It does not prove that every recommended action is finished or that monarch numbers have recovered. [UNESCO World Heritage Committee, Decision 47 COM 7B.38](https://whc.unesco.org/en/decisions/8762/).

**Learn it simply:** A **habitat** is a place where a living thing finds what it needs. A **migration** is a regular move from one place to another. A **population** is a group of the same kind of living thing. **Evidence** is information that supports a claim. A **recommendation** tells people what an organization thinks should happen; it is not proof that it already happened. Monarch conservation is a shared issue because the eastern butterflies travel across national borders and depend on different places during their life cycle. The USFWS graph is not a perfect count of every butterfly: the two panels use different measures, and survey effort matters when reading the western panel.

![Locator map for the four Grade 5 Western Hemisphere case-study countries](images/grade-05/social-studies/g05-social-western-hemisphere-locator.png)

*The local PNG locates the case-study countries only; it is not evidence about the civic issue or the monarch migration route. For this public supplement, use USFWS Figure 2.2 and Figure E1 linked above: the first is a migration map, and the second contains two differently measured population graphs. The assigned Passport issue may need different visuals. The blank evidence organizer remains listed in the image manifest; no new generated image is needed for this case study.*

**Five study sessions — 45–60 minutes each:**

1. **Read and mark the issue:** Read the USFWS summary and the UNESCO decision. Write a neutral one-sentence issue statement. Under it, list the countries and places named by each source. Keep the classroom's assigned issue in a separate box if it differs.
2. **Study the visuals:** Open USFWS Figure 2.2 (migration map) and Figure E1 (population graphs). Make a caption for each. On Figure E1, name what each population measure counts; explain why hectares and a butterfly count cannot be compared as if they were the same unit. Note the blue survey-effort line on the western graph.
3. **Compare evidence and action:** Create a two-source table: creator/date; source type; claim or finding; evidence; what it does not prove. USFWS provides a scientific status assessment. UNESCO's decision records a committee recommendation. Do not treat a recommendation as an observed result.
4. **Plan a realistic civic request:** Name a responsible audience and action supported by the sources. If using the classroom's required OAS petition format, say that the petition is a class civic exercise: the public sources here identify countries and conservation bodies, not an OAS monarch program. A request for discussion or cooperation is supportable; claiming the OAS controls a specific forest is not.
5. **Present and reflect:** Make a short evidence-based presentation or petition. Use the migration map or graph only where it helps the point. Include one source-supported concern, one proposed action, one limit, and a fair account of what more evidence is needed. If the actual Passport assignment uses a different issue, complete it with the teacher's assigned country sources instead.

**Source-based practice — use the monarch reading, USFWS figures, and UNESCO decision:**

1. How many North American migrating groups does the USFWS reading distinguish?
2. Where does the eastern group spend winter?
3. Where does the western group spend winter?
4. Does the reading say both groups follow the same route? Give one source detail.
5. What does the eastern Figure E1 panel measure?
6. What does the western Figure E1 panel measure, and what does its blue line show?
7. What broad pattern does USFWS report for both groups over the long record? What can change from year to year?
8. Name two pressures the USFWS report identifies.
9. Which three countries does UNESCO name in its cooperation decision?
10. Name two actions UNESCO encourages the countries to take.
11. Does UNESCO's recommendation prove that all actions are complete? Explain.
12. Which source is a scientific assessment and which is a policy decision?
13. Write one claim about the issue and cite one fact or graph feature that supports it.
14. Name one thing these sources do not tell us about the local issue assigned in a particular classroom.
15. Write a realistic request for action. Name the audience, cite a source fact, and state one limit or unanswered question.

**Checked answer key:**

1. **Two** North American migrating groups: eastern and western.
2. **Central Mexico.**
3. **Along the California coast** (the report also discusses northern Baja California winter sites).
4. **No.** The eastern group winters in central Mexico and moves north toward Canada over generations; western monarchs use different winter sites in California.
5. **The area occupied at eastern winter sites, measured in hectares.** It is not a direct count of individual butterflies.
6. **A total butterfly count** for the western group; the blue line shows the number of survey sites monitored.
7. Both records show **long-term declines at winter sites**, while year-to-year numbers or area can fluctuate with environmental conditions.
8. Any two: **habitat loss/degradation, insecticide exposure, or climate change.**
9. **Canada, Mexico, and the United States.**
10. Any two: **protective legislation; reduce milkweed habitat loss; restore habitat; continue trinational cooperation along the migration corridor.**
11. **No.** UNESCO encourages actions; a recommendation is not evidence that the action is complete or that the population has recovered.
12. **USFWS is the scientific species-status assessment; UNESCO's document is a World Heritage Committee decision/recommendation.**
13. Answers vary. The claim must match the source, and the cited evidence must actually support it. Example structure: “The eastern monarch uses more than one country because the report says it winters in Mexico and travels north toward Canada.”
14. Answers vary; valid limits include the exact topic/countries the teacher assigned, local population numbers, a student's own classroom schedule, or whether a recommended action has since been completed. Students should not fill an information gap with a guess.
15. Answers vary. A complete response names an audience that could reasonably discuss or support the action, uses an accurate source fact, and states a limit. Do not claim the OAS directly manages monarch habitat; the classroom petition format and real-world responsibility are different questions.

**Core civic-skill check:**

16. What four details make a neutral issue statement clear?
17. Is a strong opinion evidence?
18. Why compare sources?
19. Does a photograph alone prove why a population changed?
20. What makes a proposal usable?
21. How should a student represent a viewpoint they disagree with?
22. How should a petition end?

**Answer check:**

16. **Issue, people or living things affected, place, and time.**
17. **No; it needs facts from a source.**
18. Sources may use different evidence, answer different questions, or have different limits.
19. **No.** A photograph may show a place or moment, but causes need more evidence.
20. **A specific action, a reasonable audience, source evidence, and one limit.**
21. Describe the viewpoint accurately and fairly, cite its source, and discuss evidence without insulting people.
22. Ask for a specific action and support the request with cited facts.

**Final source check:** The public page identifies the unit's broad themes and source types, not the live issue assigned in a particular classroom. Fill in the issue, countries, evidence, and final answer from the actual NYC Passport lesson. The monarch case and added questions are public-source supplemental practice, not copied district questions.

**Extended civic-evidence lab:** Use the teacher-assigned issue to complete this organizer: (a) neutral issue statement; (b) people and places named in the sources; (c) one claim from each source; (d) the evidence each source gives; (e) a question neither source answers. **Checked sample structure:** “The sources describe [issue] in [place/time]. Source A claims __ and gives __ as evidence. Source B claims __ and gives __. I still need to learn __.” Fill every blank from the class materials.

**Extension prompts:**

- Separate a value statement (“this is fair”) from an evidence statement (“the report counted…”). **Check:** a value is a judgment; a count is evidence only when its source and method are clear.
- Name one group affected by the assigned issue and cite where a source says so. **Check:** the group and source location must match the class reading.
- Draft one action request and name an audience that could act. **Check:** the action and audience must fit the issue and evidence.
- Add one limit: what could make the proposal hard or incomplete? **Check:** name a real limit from a source or mark it as a question to research; do not promise a guaranteed result.

**Presentation rubric:** 1 point for a clear issue and place, 2 for accurately cited evidence from two perspectives, 1 for a specific request, and 1 for fair treatment of another view. If the real district task names a different audience or format, use that instruction instead of the practice structure here.

Science.title: Science week: traits, life cycles, and survival data
Science.subject: Science
Science.contentMarkdown:
**Real source:** NYSED's 2025 Grade 5 science booklet gives one connected investigation about dog traits/life stages and African wild dog pack size and pup survival. The official paper includes photos, a life-cycle model, a data table, and its scoring guide. This is a state assessment example, not a P.S. 179 textbook lesson. [NYSED Grade 5 science released questions and scoring guide](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/science/2025/2025-released-items-science-g5.pdf), questions 1–5 and scoring pages.

#### Learn the ideas from the released source

A **trait** is a feature of an organism, such as body shape or coat pattern. Offspring receive information from both parents. Siblings can inherit different combinations, so they may not look exactly alike. A photograph can show a visible trait; it cannot prove the cause of every difference. In the NYSED booklet, students compare Havanese parents and puppies, identify one visible feature shared by them, and reason about inherited information.

The same booklet explains that shedding varies by breed and age, and can also change with food, daylight, temperature, and other conditions. Its multiple-choice item asks students to identify that shedding is influenced by both inherited traits and the environment. The key idea is that a trait or change can have more than one influence; avoid “only” unless the source supports it.

A **life cycle** shows important stages in an organism's life. The released dog model uses birth, growth, and reproduction. These are broad stages, not a claim that all animals have identical details. Read the model's arrows and labels; do not add unshown stages to an answer about that specific diagram.

The booklet then gives real research data on African wild dog packs in Tanzania. Researchers studied 11 packs during 1991–1996 and recorded adult pack size and pup survival. The table reports an average fraction of pups out of ten that survived to at least one year. NYSED's scoring guide gives a valid comparison: packs with 4 adults had an average of 4 pups out of 10 survive, while packs with 17 adults averaged 9 out of 10. This supports a pattern in that dataset. It does not prove that adding adults alone caused the difference, or that every pack everywhere will have the same result.

| Day | 45–60-minute lesson and work |
|---|---|
| 1 — Read traits in a photo | Read the booklet's dog-and-puppy description and inspect its actual photo. Answer Questions 1 and 2. Mark the exact visible evidence for a shared trait; separate what the photo shows from what Question 1 says about inherited information. |
| 2 — Compare influences | Read the released text about shedding. Answer Question 3. Make two columns for factors named by the source: inherited/breed-related and environmental or other conditions. Explain why “only inherited” and “only environment” are incomplete. |
| 3 — Model a life cycle | Study the dog life-cycle model and answer Question 4. Rewrite its stages in order with arrows. Describe what each stage label means; use the source rather than adding a new stage. |
| 4 — Read the survival table | Read the table title, units, place, time span, and population studied. Compare pack sizes and fractions of pups surviving out of ten. Write the two values as fractions and explain what the denominator 10 means. |
| 5 — Make a careful argument | Answer Question 5 with a claim and two table values. Read NYSED's scoring guide. Revise any statement that says the pattern proves cause or applies to every wild dog pack. |

#### Supplemental practice — newly written from the official source data

Use the released booklet's Questions 1–5, photo, model, table, and scoring guide. The first five are authentic NYSED item tasks described in new words; the remaining prompts are new study questions.

1. What kind of information did each puppy inherit, according to Question 1?
2. Name one body feature the NYSED scoring guide accepts as visible in both parents and offspring.
3. What two broad kinds of influence does Question 3 say affect shedding?
4. Put the three stages in the dog model in their correct order.
5. In the wild-dog data, compare 4 adults and 17 adults. How many pups out of ten survived on average in each pack size?
6. In “4 out of 10 pups,” what does 10 represent?
7. Write a sentence that describes the direction of the pattern in the table.
8. Does the table prove that pack size alone caused the survival difference? Why or why not?
9. Name the place, years, and number of packs in the study. Why should a reader include these details when explaining what the table shows?
10. The source says shedding can vary with age, diet, daylight, and temperature as well as breed. Give one example of a non-inherited influence named in the passage.
11. Write a question about pup survival that this table cannot answer by itself.
12. Write a claim about pack size and survival. Include two values from the table and one limitation of the evidence.

questions.prompt: After trying the practice above, briefly note that you are ready to compare your work with the guide’s checked responses.

Science.answerKeyMarkdown:
#### Checked answer key

1. **Different information from both parents.** This is choice A in Question 1.
2. **Any one visible shared trait accepted by NYSED:** body shape, similar face shape, or the same number of eyes/ears. The answer must match the actual photo.
3. **Inherited traits and the environment.** This is choice C in Question 3.
4. **Birth → growth → reproduction.** This is choice B in Question 4.
5. **4 adults: 4/10; 17 adults: 9/10.** These are averages in the released table.
6. **The ten pups used as the whole group for the fraction.** Four of those ten, on average, survived to at least one year in the 4-adult-pack data.
7. **In this study, larger adult packs tended to have a larger fraction of pups survive to one year.** The claim is limited to these data.
8. **No.** The table shows a relationship/pattern but does not isolate pack size as the only cause.
9. **Tanzania, 1991–1996, 11 packs.** These limits tell the reader where, when, and how many packs the findings describe.
10. **Any source-supported example:** age, diet, daylight, or temperature.
11. **Answers vary:** examples include why the packs differ, what happened in a different place/year, or whether another factor affected survival. The table alone does not answer these.
12. **Answers vary.** A strong answer uses two accurate table values, describes the pattern, and says it applies to the studied packs/time rather than all packs.

If the source image or table is not available, do not guess which trait is visible or invent additional data. The official paper and scoring guide are the answer source for the released item.

Science.title: Science week: matter, new substances, evaporation, and mineral properties
Science.subject: Science
Science.contentMarkdown:
**Real source:** the Spring 2025 NYSED Grade 5 science booklet uses a sealed iron-and-water investigation and a Jones Beach mineral sample. Questions 6–10 ask students to identify evidence of a new substance, use mass evidence, model evaporation, use material properties to separate magnetite, and read a beach-sand graph. The booklet includes its official rating guide. This is authentic state assessment content, not a P.S. 179 textbook sequence. [NYSED 2025 Grade 5 science released questions, pp. 6–9 and rating guide](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/science/2025/2025-released-items-science-g5.pdf).

#### Learn the ideas from the released source

A **property** is something about a material that can be observed or tested, such as color, magnetism, or whether light passes through it. A property can help identify a material or separate it from a mixture. The NYSED booklet's beach-sand section uses a table of magnetite, garnet, and quartz properties, then asks students to choose a way to separate magnetite. The source-supported choice uses a magnet because magnetite is magnetic while the listed garnet and quartz are not.

In the booklet's first investigation, students put water and iron filings in a sealed container. The filings changed from black to dark red. That color change is evidence that a new substance formed. It is an **observation** to say “the color changed”; it is an **inference** to say a new substance formed because of the change. Scientists use more than one piece of evidence when possible.

The starting container has a mass of 25 grams. The water has a mass of 5 grams, and the iron has a mass of 5 grams. Together, 25 + 5 + 5 = **35 grams**. The sealed container and contents measure 35 grams the next day. This supports the idea that matter is conserved in the closed system: the total matter did not disappear when the substances changed.

When the container is opened, water can change from liquid to water vapor and move into the air. This process is **evaporation**. The water has not vanished; it has moved into the air as gas. The test booklet asks students to choose a particle model for the unsealed container after a week. The official scoring guide identifies Model B and evaporation. Use the original booklet image to match the actual model; do not substitute a recreated particle drawing.

The booklet also gives a pie graph about sand from Westhampton Beach. A graph key explains the categories. The official rating guide accepts two observations: the sample has more red particles and fewer magnetic particles than the comparison. When you read a graph, match each color/slice to its legend and say “more” or “fewer” only after comparing the correct categories.

| Day | 45–60-minute lesson and work |
|---|---|
| 1 — Observe a change | Read NYSED Questions 6–7. Make a before/after table for the iron's color and the container's mass. Mark which statements are direct observations and which are explanations. Explain why the color evidence matters. |
| 2 — Follow the mass | Add the starting masses with units. Compare that total with the final measured mass. Write a short claim about conservation in this sealed system and cite both numbers. Explain what could make an open-container measurement harder to compare. |
| 3 — Model evaporation | Read Question 8 and inspect the source's particle-model choices. Choose the official model, name evaporation, and draw an arrow showing where water moves when the container is open. Explain why “the water disappeared” is not a complete explanation. |
| 4 — Separate a mixture | Study the actual mineral table in Questions 9–10. Make a property chart for magnetite, garnet, and quartz. Choose a tool based on a property shown in the table. Explain why color alone is not the best reason if the source identifies magnetism as the distinguishing property. |
| 5 — Interpret the beach-sand graph | Read the graph title, key, and categories. Compare red and magnetic particles in Westhampton Beach sand with the comparison in the official figure. Write two observations supported by the scoring guide and one question the graph does not answer. |

#### Supplemental practice — newly written, based on the official booklet

1. What color were the iron filings before the investigation, and what color were some afterward?
2. Which observation is evidence that a new substance formed?
3. Calculate the starting mass of the sealed setup: container 25 g, water 5 g, iron 5 g.
4. The next day's sealed total is 35 g. What does this support about matter in the system?
5. Does a color change by itself tell every detail about what substance formed? Explain.
6. Name the process that moves liquid water into the air as water vapor.
7. The original booklet's correct model for water after the container is opened is B. What process does the official key name?
8. If water evaporates from an open container, has the water ceased to exist? Explain where it went.
9. Which property supports using a magnet to separate magnetite from the listed garnet and quartz?
10. The Westhampton Beach graph shows more red particles than the comparison. Is this a graph observation or an explanation? What part of the graph should you check?
11. Name the two observations accepted by the official scoring guide for the Westhampton sample.
12. Write one sentence about what the source's investigation shows, using one measurement and one limitation.

questions.prompt: After trying the practice above, briefly note that you are ready to compare your work with the guide’s checked responses.

Science.answerKeyMarkdown:
#### Checked answer key

1. **Black before; some filings were dark red afterward.**
2. **The color changed from black to dark red.** NYSED's scoring guide accepts this as evidence of a new substance.
3. **35 g:** 25 + 5 + 5.
4. **It supports conservation of matter in the sealed system:** the measured total remained 35 g.
5. **No.** The color change is evidence of a change; more evidence would be needed to identify every detail of the new substance.
6. **Evaporation.**
7. **Evaporation.**
8. **No.** It becomes water vapor and moves into the air.
9. **Magnetism:** magnetite is magnetic, unlike the listed garnet and quartz.
10. **It is an observation/comparison.** Check the graph key and ensure the red category is read correctly.
11. **More red particles and fewer magnetic particles.**
12. **Answers vary.** Require one correct source measurement and a limitation, such as the test used one sealed setup or the graph describes a particular sand sample.

The exact model choices and graph categories are in the linked state booklet; keep them visible while answering. This unit uses NYSED released material and state-aligned practice, not a claim about P.S. 179's assigned textbook.

Science.title: Science week: earthquake patterns, New York evidence, and safer buildings
Science.subject: Science
Science.contentMarkdown:
**Real source:** the same NYSED booklet has a five-question cluster on earthquakes, volcanoes, a New York damage map, and engineering choices for New York City buildings (questions 11–15). Its official rating guide gives the accepted map-based reasoning. This is a state test example, not proof of a current P.S. 179 class unit. [NYSED 2025 Grade 5 science released questions, pp. 10–13 and rating guide](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/science/2025/2025-released-items-science-g5.pdf).

#### Learn the real map and passage

An **earthquake** is shaking of the ground. A **volcano** is an opening where hot melted rock and gases can come out. A map can show where earthquakes and volcanoes have occurred; a **pattern** is a repeated arrangement in those marks. In NYSED's 2025 booklet, many earthquake and volcano marks appear in similar places near the Ring of Fire. The map supports “many occur in similar locations.” It does not support “every earthquake happens at a volcano” or “every boundary has earthquakes.”

The test asks readers to compare the map evidence for Oregon and New York. Oregon is near the Ring of Fire, and the source map shows earthquake marks there; it shows no marks in New York. The answer is a comparison of the evidence printed in that source, not a promise that an earthquake will or will not happen in either state.

A second map shows the chance of earthquake **damage** across New York State. The source says its categories are based on how often earthquakes have occurred at a location and the strength of the ground shaking people felt. Its legend ranges from low chance (rarely felt) to medium-high chance (easily felt by all). The released item identifies the northeast region as having the greatest chance on that map. That category does not mean other places never have earthquakes: the passage says small earthquakes occur throughout the state.

The NYC building passage says the city has many buildings, including older ones that may not have been reinforced for earthquake shaking. It discusses how ground and building features affect shaking and provides five proposed actions. In the released item, the keyed pair is to reinforce brick buildings/repair foundations and design new interior walls to absorb forces. This is the state test's evidence-based answer. It is not a substitute for current building codes or professional engineering advice.

When answering, separate **map observation** (“the dots are near this region”) from **inference** (“these data show a pattern”) and from a **prediction** (“an earthquake will occur here next year”). The released map supports the first two; it does not give an exact date or guarantee a future event.

| Day | 45–60-minute lesson and work |
|---|---|
| 1 — Read the world map | Use the test's Ring of Fire map and key. Locate New York, Oregon, the Pacific, earthquake marks, volcanoes, and the marked boundary. Write three direct observations before explaining what they might mean. |
| 2 — Compare earthquake and volcano marks | Compare the two map patterns. Write one similarity using “many” or “often,” then add one limit explaining why the map does not show that every earthquake has a nearby volcano. Use the legend to support each statement. |
| 3 — Compare Oregon and New York | Read the question passage and map together. State which has the greater chance of a destructive earthquake in this source and cite a map or passage detail. Keep the response about the evidence shown; do not forecast a date. |
| 4 — Interpret the New York damage map | Read every category in the legend, then identify the region with the highest category. Find the passage sentence explaining how the map's damage categories were made. Explain the difference between “earthquakes occur” and “chance of damage.” |
| 5 — Evaluate building choices | Read all five proposed actions in the booklet. Circle the two the official key accepts, then explain how each addresses damage to buildings. Write one caution: the released test is a classroom source, not a current construction standard. |

#### Supplemental practice — newly written from the NYSED map set

Answer while looking at Questions 11–15 and their maps. These prompts restate or extend the published evidence; they are not a current local hazard report.

1. According to the world map, where do most earthquakes occur: the centers of continents, centers of oceans, some ocean-continent boundaries, or all such boundaries?
2. What general relationship does the booklet show between earthquake and volcano locations?
3. Which state has the greater chance of a destructive earthquake in the source comparison, New York or Oregon? Name one map clue.
4. Which region of New York State has the highest chance-of-damage category on the test map?
5. Which two proposed building solutions are correct in NYSED Question 15?
6. What does “low chance of damage, earthquake rarely felt” tell you? What does it not tell you?
7. The passage says small earthquakes occur throughout New York State. Does that conflict with the damage map? Explain.
8. Is “there are no earthquake marks in New York on the Ring of Fire map” a direct observation or a prediction?
9. Why must you read the legend before deciding which NY region has the highest chance of damage?
10. Name one statement the map does not prove about the next earthquake.
11. Why is “many earthquakes and volcanoes occur in similar locations” more accurate than “all earthquakes happen next to volcanoes”?
12. Write a three-sentence source-based summary: one world-map pattern, one New York damage-map fact, and one building action accepted by the test key.

questions.prompt: After trying the practice above, briefly note that you are ready to compare your work with the guide’s checked responses.

Science.answerKeyMarkdown:
#### Checked answer guide

1. **Along some boundaries where oceans and continents meet.** This is Question 11, choice C; “some” matters.
2. **Many occur in similar locations, especially along the Ring of Fire.**
3. **Oregon.** The map shows earthquake marks there near the Ring of Fire and none in New York.
4. **Northeast New York.** This is Question 14, choice B.
5. **Solutions 1 and 2.** Reinforce brick buildings/repair foundations, and design new interior walls to absorb forces. This is Question 15, choice A.
6. **It describes the map's low damage category and that earthquakes there are rarely felt.** It does not say an earthquake is impossible.
7. **No.** One source says small earthquakes occur throughout the state; the map ranks chances of damage. Occurrence and damage chance are different.
8. **A direct observation about the displayed map.** It does not predict that New York will never have an earthquake.
9. **The legend defines the categories.** Without it, colors cannot be matched to levels of chance.
10. **Answers vary:** exact date, exact location, or certainty that a building will/will not be damaged are examples.
11. **The map shows a repeated pattern with exceptions/limits.** “All” is stronger than the evidence.
12. **Answers vary.** Each sentence must match the relevant map/passage, and the building action must be one of the two accepted by NYSED's key.

Check every comparison against the map key and passage. A map category is a summary of evidence; it is not a guarantee about one future event.

Science.title: Science week: matter and energy in the Albany Pine Bush ecosystem
Science.subject: Science
Science.contentMarkdown:
**Real source:** NYSED's Spring 2025 Grade 5 science test uses a case study of the Albany Pine Bush and gives a passage, organism images, a matter model, life-cycle models, a range map, and controlled-burn facts in questions 21–25. The details below are tied to that source. They are not a claim about Taha's current P.S. 179 unit. [NYSED released test and rating guide, questions 21–25, PDF pp. 18–22](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/science/2025/2025-released-items-science-g5.pdf).

**Visual status:** the delivered food-web PNG is a blank organizer that says no species were supplied. Keep it out of the lesson as a finished web. The source list is now verified against NYSED's booklet and rating guide, and the image manifest records the source-based replacement. The released test's bacteria diagram is a **matter model**; keep its decomposer arrows separate from food-to-consumer energy arrows.

#### Source reading in simple English

The NYSED test describes the Albany Pine Bush, an inland area in Albany, New York. Its sandy habitat is unusual because this kind of ecosystem is usually found near a coast. Part of the area is protected. The passage identifies the endangered Karner blue butterfly and wild blue lupine there. The Karner blue caterpillar's only food source is wild blue lupine. The seven-spotted ladybug is one of the few confirmed predators of that caterpillar, and it feeds only on animals.

The test also describes the frosted elfin butterfly. Its caterpillar and the Karner blue caterpillar both depend on wild blue lupine, but they eat different parts: the Karner blue caterpillar eats leaves; the frosted elfin caterpillar eats flowers and seed pods. The preserve covers about 3,000 acres. A map in the test shows places where the frosted elfin was observed in New York in 2018 and the mapped Karner blue habitat. The test asks students to compare those patterns, not to guess from the butterflies' names.

The NYSED passage says natural wildfires once helped keep this habitat suitable for lupine and other native plants. To protect homes, most wildfires are now put out quickly. The Albany Pine Bush Preserve Commission uses controlled burns. The test lists benefits in this preserve: removing invasive species, clearing leaves and twigs so seeds can grow in sandy soil, keeping areas from becoming covered by large trees, and opening some pine seed pods. These details support a claim about this place; they do not prove that all fires help all ecosystems.

#### Keep matter and energy diagrams separate

In a **food-energy web**, arrows point from food to the organism that eats it. For the verified links in this source, draw:

```text
sunlight → wild blue lupine → Karner blue caterpillar → seven-spotted ladybug
                          ↘ frosted elfin caterpillar
```

The source says light is the plant's energy source. Do not draw sunlight as food, and do not draw an arrow from the ladybug back to the plant.

The released test also asks about a **matter movement model**. Its rating guide shows air and water leading to the lupine; lupine, caterpillars, and ladybugs connected to bacteria; and bacteria leading to decomposed material. That model tracks matter, including decomposition. It is not the same diagram as the simpler food-energy web. The current delivered blank template can be used to practice labels or arrows only after its prompt matches the model being taught.

#### Five study sessions

| Session | 45–60-minute lesson and work | End check |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Read and collect facts | Read the actual NYSED passage on PDF pp. 18–22. Build a source table with each named organism, what the text says it eats or does, and a page number. Mark “not stated” when the source gives no relationship. | Every organism claim can be pointed to in the released passage or diagram. |
| 2 — Build the food-energy web | Use the verified source list. Draw lupine, both caterpillars, and the ladybug. Add arrows from food to consumer and write that rule beside the diagram. Keep bacteria in a separate matter box. | Trace one complete energy path and explain why each arrow points that way. |
| 3 — Read the matter model | Inspect the original NYSED diagram and rating guide. Label air/water, plant, consumers, bacteria, and decomposed material. Describe how matter reaches the decomposer without saying that energy cycles back to the plant. | The learner can tell what the model tracks and how it differs from the food-energy web. |
| 4 — Compare life-cycle and range evidence | Study the booklet's two life-cycle models and the 2018 observation map. Write one comparison from the models and one map-based claim about the butterflies' mapped ranges. | Each statement names the model/map evidence; no range is claimed outside the date and place shown. |
| 5 — Explain habitat care | Read the controlled-burn list. Write a claim about how burns may help keep this preserve suitable for lupine, then connect lupine to caterpillar food using the passage. Include one limit: this claim is about the Albany Pine Bush evidence. | Claim, two source details, and the limit all match the booklet. |

#### Official released-item checks

These are answer checks for NYSED's released questions, not replacement questions: **Q21** is the matter model with all four organisms placed as shown in the rating guide; **Q22 is D**, light is captured and changed into a form the lupine can use; **Q23 is C**, the two butterflies have similar stages but differ in their modeled yearly timing/growth pattern; **Q24** selects the **frosted elfin butterfly**, supported by the map showing observations in more New York areas while the Karner blue is shown in one habitat; **Q25 is A**, controlled burns maintain conditions that allow lupine to grow and provide food for the Karner blue caterpillar. Check each response against the source diagram and map, not memory.

#### Practice set — new evidence questions using the real NYSED source

1. Is the Albany Pine Bush described as inland or coastal? What detail makes it unusual?
2. Name the Karner blue caterpillar's only food source.
3. Which part of the lupine does each caterpillar eat?
4. What animal is named as a confirmed predator of the Karner blue caterpillar?
5. Draw the three-step food-energy path from sunlight to the ladybug. State what each arrow means.
6. In the test's matter model, what does bacteria do? Where does the diagram show matter going after bacteria?
7. Why should the food-energy arrows and matter-model arrows not be combined without labels?
8. What map evidence supports choosing the frosted elfin in question 24? Include the map's date clue.
9. Name two benefits of controlled burns listed by the test passage.
10. Write one claim about controlled burns in the Albany Pine Bush and support it with two details from the source.
11. A student says, “Fire always helps every ecosystem.” Explain why the released passage does not support that claim.
12. Name one question about this ecosystem that the released test does not answer. Write what extra source or observation you would need.

Science.answerKeyMarkdown:
#### Checked answer key

1. **Inland.** It is unusual because the passage says this sandy ecosystem is normally found in coastal areas.
2. **Wild blue lupine.** The released passage calls it the caterpillar's only food source.
3. The Karner blue caterpillar eats **leaves**; the frosted elfin caterpillar eats **flowers and seed pods**.
4. The **seven-spotted ladybug**; the source calls it one of the few confirmed predators.
5. **Sunlight → lupine → Karner blue caterpillar → seven-spotted ladybug.** Arrows point from the energy source/food to the organism receiving energy by using it or eating it. Lupine also feeds the frosted elfin caterpillar, but that branch is not needed for this path.
6. **Bacteria decompose matter** in the model; the rating-guide diagram shows matter going to **decomposed material**.
7. One is a food-energy path; the other represents matter movement and decomposition. Without labels, a reader could mistake matter return for energy flowing backward to the plant.
8. The 2018 map shows frosted elfin observations across more New York areas, while the Karner blue is shown in one habitat. The claim must be tied to that map, not generalized to every place or year.
9. Any two from the source: remove invasive species; clear leaves/twigs so seeds can grow; keep areas from being taken over by large trees; open pine seed pods.
10. Answers vary. A strong response says controlled burns help maintain conditions for lupine, then cites two listed effects and the passage's link between lupine and caterpillar food.
11. The test gives evidence about one managed preserve. It does not compare every ecosystem or every kind of fire, so “always” is too broad.
12. Answers vary. Accept a focused unanswered question and a source/observation that could answer it; do not treat the missing information as a known fact.

**Mastery check:** the student cites the released reading, diagram, or dated map; draws food-energy arrows in the correct direction; keeps matter cycling separate; and limits habitat claims to what the Albany Pine Bush source shows.

Science.title: Science week: Sun, Earth, Moon, stars, and repeating patterns
Science.subject: Science
Science.contentMarkdown:
**Real source:** NYSED’s 2025 Grade 5 science booklet uses measured star distances, a year-long constellation model, Earth’s tilted orbit, and a month of Moon observations (questions 26–30). The packet includes actual diagrams, photographs, and its official rating guide. These are state-test materials, not P.S. 179 textbook pages. [NYSED 2025 Grade 5 science released questions, pp. 20–24 and rating guide](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/science/2025/2025-released-items-science-g5.pdf).

#### Learn the ideas in the NYSED models

The released booklet uses a real measurement called an **astronomical unit (AU)**. In its table, the Sun is 1 AU from Earth, Alpha Centauri A and B are about 13,000 AU away, and Beta Pavonis is about 8,600,000 AU away. The question asks why the Sun appears brighter and larger from Earth even though these stars can be much larger than the Sun. The numerical evidence is distance: the listed stars are far, far farther away. A picture of apparent size does not show a star's actual size.

Some stars appear to form patterns called **constellations**. The booklet's orbit model shows some constellations visible from New York in different months. As Earth orbits the Sun, the night side faces different directions in space over the year. People therefore see different parts of the sky in different seasons. The model shows a yearly repeating pattern; it does not mean the stars are attached to a spinning sky around Earth.

Earth also rotates on its axis. Rotation causes day and night. Earth's axis is tilted, and Earth keeps that tilt as it orbits the Sun. The booklet's model compares daylight at the North Pole on June 21 and December 21: it shows less daylight in December because Earth is tilted. Keep the causes separate: rotation gives day/night; the orbit and tilted axis help explain yearly sky/daylight patterns.

The booklet also uses photographs taken during June 2018 to show the Moon's appearance over one month. The visible part changes in a repeating pattern. Use the actual dated photo calendar and the graph choices in the released test; do not copy a present-day Moon calendar from memory. The test's graph key identifies the choice that fits those 2018 observations. A single photograph shows one date, while the sequence makes the repeating pattern visible.

| Day | 45–60-minute lesson and work |
|---|---|

2. **13,000 AU.**
3. **8,600,000 AU.**

Science.title: Science week: static electricity, balanced forces, and evidence from trials
Science.subject: Science
Science.contentMarkdown:
**Scope note:** the NYSED Grade 5 released booklet includes questions aligned to earlier Grade 3–5 band expectations; this week is a **cumulative standards review** based on the actual 2025 balloon investigations, not a claim that P.S. 179 teaches a separate Grade 5 static-electricity unit. [NYSED 2025 Grade 5 science released questions, pp. 25–29 and rating guide](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/science/2025/2025-released-items-science-g5.pdf).

#### Learn the ideas from the real balloon investigations

A **force** is a push or pull. In the first released figure, two balloons are hanging at rest before the student rubs them. The scoring guide accepts **balanced** forces because the evidence is that a balloon is not moving. “Balanced” does not mean no forces exist; gravity and the string's support act on the balloon, and its motion does not change.

The student rubs both balloons with wool in the same direction. The released test identifies the result as each balloon becoming electrically charged and moving away from the other balloon. It is an electric interaction, not magnetism. Use the source figure and answer key; do not add an unseen charge-transfer path between the two balloons.

In the next investigation, a rubbed balloon is lowered toward small paper pieces. The changed variable is the balloon's distance/height from the paper. A clear test question includes that variable, such as asking how distance affects the interaction. When the paper moves upward, the test's correct explanation is that the balloon's force on the paper is greater than gravity's force on it. The visible motion is evidence the forces are not balanced in that moment.

Repeating a test can show whether its result is reliable. In the released item, both balloons used in the repeat are the same material, size, and color; the point of another trial is to check the reliability of the first result, not to test all those properties. Keep the changed variable clear and record each trial.

In the third investigation, a rubbed balloon is held near a metal can and the can rolls toward it. The observed movement is evidence that energy changed into the can's motion. The answer is about evidence from this trial; the question does not ask the student to measure how much energy moved.

If repeating any classroom activity, use teacher-approved materials, keep small paper pieces away from mouths, and avoid water/electronics. Record what happened rather than predicting a result and calling it data.

| Day | 45–60-minute lesson and work |
|---|---|
| 1 — Balanced forces | Read NYSED Figure 1. Decide balanced/unbalanced and underline the evidence about motion. Draw an arrow model for gravity and string support; explain why “at rest” is evidence for no change in motion, not for “no forces.” |
| 2 — Electric charge | Read the wool-and-balloon procedure and Figures 2–3. Make a before/during/after chart. State what was changed, what moved, and which cause the state key accepts. Explain why “became magnetic” does not match the answer key. |
| 3 — Change distance | Read the paper-and-balloon setup and identify distance/height as the changed variable. Write two testable questions, each using that variable. If doing a teacher-approved trial, use equal-size papers and a ruler, change one distance at a time, and record the actual result. |
| 4 — Explain motion and forces | Use the paper-lifting figure. Draw a downward gravity arrow and an upward balloon-force arrow. Explain which force is greater while the paper moves upward and how its motion supports that explanation. |
| 5 — Reliability and energy | Explain why a repeat trial uses the same balloon properties. Study the can trial and identify the observed evidence of energy conversion. Write a short summary using one claim, one observation, and one test limitation. |

#### Supplemental practice — newly written from NYSED Questions 31–36

Use the actual test figures and official rating guide. New activity data must come from a learner's own safe trial.

1. In Figure 1, a balloon hangs still. Are the forces balanced or unbalanced? What observed detail supports the answer?
2. Does “balanced” mean there are no forces on the balloon? Explain.
3. What happened to the two balloons after both were rubbed with wool?
4. Which explanation does the source support: electric charge or magnetism?
5. What variable changes as a rubbed balloon is lowered toward small paper pieces?
6. Write a testable question about that variable. Include a question mark.
7. When the paper moves upward toward the balloon, which force is greater in the NYSED explanation: the balloon's force or gravity?
8. Does the moving paper show balanced or unbalanced forces? Explain using its motion.
9. Why should a student repeat the paper-and-balloon investigation?
10. In the can trial, what observation is evidence of energy conversion?
11. A student changes distance and balloon material at the same time. Why will this make the result harder to explain?
12. Write a claim about one actual trial. Add the observation and one limit; leave the result blank until the trial is done.

questions.prompt: After trying the practice above, briefly note that you are ready to compare your work with the guide’s checked responses.

Science.answerKeyMarkdown:
#### Checked answer key

1. **Balanced.** The balloon is at rest/not moving in Figure 1.
2. **No.** Forces can act while balanced; the evidence is that the balloon's motion does not change.
3. **They moved away from each other after becoming electrically charged.** This is Question 32, choice A.
4. **Electric charge.** The official answer is not magnetism.
5. **Distance/height/closeness between the balloon and the paper.**
6. **Answers vary.** For example: “How does the balloon's distance from the paper affect the paper's movement?” It has to be a question about distance.
7. **The balloon's force.** It must be greater than gravity for the paper to move upward in the source's explanation.
8. **Unbalanced.** Its motion changes upward.
9. **To check the reliability of the first result.** This is Question 35, choice B.
10. **The can rolls across the table.** This is Question 36, choice C.
11. **Two variables changed, so the student cannot tell which change affected the result.**
12. **Answers depend on the learner's trial.** Require an observed result and one honest limit; do not fill in a predicted outcome as data.

Official answer labels: Question 31 balanced; 32 A; 34 D; 35 B; 36 C. Question 33 requires a distance/height variable and a matching research question. See NYSED's rating guide for exact scoring.

Science.title: Science week: how Earth’s systems connect through the water cycle
Science.subject: Science
Science.contentMarkdown:
![Unlabeled landscape model shows land and soil, water, air space, plants, and animals](images/grade-05/science/g05-science-earth-systems.png)

Use the picture to identify the geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere. The arrows are unlabeled: add process words only after checking their direction against the linked NASA diagram and text.

**Scope:** New York State Grade 5 science asks students to model interactions among Earth’s geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere. NASA’s water-cycle source describes water moving among Earth’s surface, air, and living things. P.S. 179 has not published a Grade 5 science unit calendar, so this is state-aligned supplemental work. [NYS P–12 Science Learning Standards](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/curriculum-instruction/p-12-science-learning-standards.pdf) · [NASA: The Water Cycle](https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/the-water-cycle/).

#### Learn the system names and real water paths

Earth has connected systems. The **geosphere** is solid Earth, including rock and soil. The **hydrosphere** is water in oceans, lakes, rivers, groundwater, ice, and other places. The **atmosphere** is the air around Earth. The **biosphere** includes living things. A single event can connect several systems: rain falls from air onto soil, runs into a river, and can be taken up by a plant.

Water can change state and move between these systems. **Evaporation** changes liquid surface water into water vapor, which moves into the atmosphere. The Sun supplies energy that helps drive the cycle. **Condensation** happens when water vapor cools and forms tiny liquid droplets. **Precipitation** is water falling from clouds as rain, snow, sleet, or hail. After precipitation, water may flow over land as **runoff**, soak into soil and groundwater, collect in water bodies, evaporate again, or be taken up by living things. **Transpiration** is water vapor released by plants through their leaves, connecting the biosphere to the atmosphere.

NASA explains that these are parts of a continuous exchange among ocean, atmosphere, and land. The paths branch. Do not draw one neat loop as if all water takes the same route or the same amount of time. NASA gives a possible long path in which water from Lake Superior could rise into the atmosphere and later fall as rain in Massachusetts. This is an example of a possible route, not tracking of one identified water molecule.

The delivered picture is an **unlabeled model**. First name visible examples of land/rock, water, air, plants, and animals. Then add labels and arrows only when their directions match NASA's source. A model makes a large system easier to see; it leaves out details such as exact temperatures, wind, time, and the many routes water can take.

| Day | 45–60-minute lesson and work |
|---|---|
| 1 — Name the systems | Read NASA's water-cycle explanation and inspect its actual diagram. Make a four-column chart for the geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere. Record two examples for each from the source and explain why each belongs there. |
| 2 — Trace surface-to-air water | Trace one path from a water surface through evaporation, condensation, and precipitation. Add runoff or soaking in as a possible next step. Use NASA's diagram to check every arrow direction. |
| 3 — Connect plants and air | Read NASA's description of transpiration. Add a plant to your model. Show water moving from soil into a plant and water vapor moving from the plant to air. Explain how this connects the biosphere, hydrosphere, geosphere, and atmosphere. |
| 4 — Compare several routes | Make three possible pathways after rain: runoff to a stream; soaking into soil; and uptake by a plant followed by transpiration. For each, name the systems connected and use a NASA detail. |
| 5 — Revise and explain a model | Label the delivered blank picture or draw your own model. Include all four Earth systems, four process labels, and at least two branching routes. Write a paragraph explaining one path and one thing the model leaves out. |

#### Supplemental practice — newly written from NASA's source

1. Which Earth system includes soil and solid rock?
2. Which system includes rivers, lakes, and groundwater?
3. Which system includes the air surrounding Earth?
4. Which system includes plants and animals?
5. Liquid water at a surface changes to water vapor. Name the process.
6. Water vapor cools into small liquid droplets. Name the process.
7. Water falls from a cloud as rain. Name the process.
8. Give two routes water might take after it falls on land.
9. How do plants move some water from the biosphere to the atmosphere?
10. NASA describes a possible route from Lake Superior to rain in Massachusetts. Which systems can be connected along that path?
11. Does this route mean NASA tracked one named water molecule? Explain.
12. Draw two different paths through the water cycle. Include at least three systems in each path and name one limit of your model.

#### Checked answer key

1. **Geosphere.**
2. **Hydrosphere.**
3. **Atmosphere.**
4. **Biosphere.**
5. **Evaporation.**
6. **Condensation.**
7. **Precipitation.**
8. **Answers vary:** runoff to a stream/river; soak into soil/groundwater; collect in a lake; evaporate; or be taken up by a plant. The source supports multiple routes.
9. **Transpiration:** plants release water vapor from leaves.
10. **Hydrosphere, atmosphere, and geosphere** are involved in the cited possible route; a plant route can also involve the biosphere.
11. **No.** NASA describes a possible path, not tracking of one particular molecule.

4. **The Western Hemisphere Today**

The work is organized around geographic and historical comparisons, including how people and societies interact with their environments and with one another. Use the actual Passport guide/workbook for the assigned source readings and evidence tasks. [NYC Grade 5 Passport materials](https://sites.google.com/schools.nyc.gov/social-studies-and-civics/resources-by-grade/elementary/5th-grade); [Passport scope-and-sequence description](https://sites.google.com/schools.nyc.gov/social-studies-and-civics/resources/passport-to-social-studies).

### Topic-by-topic source work

- **Geography/early societies:** connect landforms, climate, water, and resources to evidence in a map or source text; avoid treating the Western Hemisphere as one uniform place.
- **European exploration:** compare accounts from different participants and identify whose perspective each source represents.
- **Comparative case study:** use the Passport's named country case studies; compare a shared question across the sources rather than generalizing from one example to a whole population.
- **Western Hemisphere today:** use current maps only for present-day borders and cite the date/source of any statistics.

The Passport workbooks provide the actual source passages and lesson questions; these bullets explain how to work with those sources, not a replacement reading.

## Science

P.S. 179 has not published a current Grade 5 science book or unit map. The state Grade 5 standards and official science test resources cover these topics:

- **Matter:** properties, particle model, and evidence that matter is conserved when materials change.
- **Earth systems:** interactions among geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere; water and Earth processes.
- **Ecosystems:** matter/energy movement and how organisms depend on their environment.
- **Sun–Earth–Moon patterns:** apparent motion, shadows, day/night, and seasonal patterns.
- **Human impacts and engineering:** use evidence to describe environmental effects and consider ways to reduce them.

NYSED publishes real Grade 5 science sample/released questions, unlike grades without a state science exam. Use the [official NYSED released science questions](https://www.nysed.gov/state-assessment/past-grades-3-8-tests) and the [Grade 5 science performance descriptions/standards](https://www.nysed.gov/state-assessment/nys-grades-3-8-science-learning-standards). These are state materials, not P.S. 179 textbook chapters.

### Exact released science example: inherited variation

The 2025 NYSED Grade 5 science booklet begins with **Traits and Survival of Dogs**. Its first question shows Havanese puppies and their parents and asks students to reason that puppies inherit traits from their parents. Use the original page's photographs to compare visible traits; do not infer that every visible difference is inherited without evidence. [2025 Grade 5 science booklet, opening item](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/science/2025/2025-released-items-science-g5.pdf).
